t.7.28.1: Seeing Sumālin slain by Vasu and reduced to ashes, and observing his own army put to flight, tormented by arrows,
t.7.28.2: Then the mighty Meghanāda, son of Rāvaṇa, enraged, turned back all the Rākṣasas and stood firm in battle.
t.7.28.3: That great chariot-warrior, in his fire-colored chariot that moved at will, rushed upon that army, blazing like a fire sweeping through the forests.
t.7.28.4: Then, as he entered bearing weapons of many kinds, the gods, at the very sight of him, fled away in all directions.
t.7.28.5: No one stood firm there in battle against him as he pressed eagerly to fight. Seeing all of them struck and terrified, Śakra spoke.
t.7.28.7: Then the god Jayanta, renowned as the son of Śakra, advanced into the battle on a chariot that was almost a marvel.
t.7.28.6: Do not be afraid, do not run away; turn back toward the battle! Here goes my son, the unconquered one, to fight.
t.7.28.8: Then all those gods, surrounding the son of Śacī, encountered the son of Rāvaṇa in battle and stood firm, arrayed for the fight.
t.7.28.10: Then the son of the Rākṣasa rained down gold-adorned arrows upon Gomukha, the son of Mātali, who was serving as charioteer.
t.7.28.9: A great and evenly matched battle arose among those gods and rākṣasas, for the sake of the son of Mahendra and the son of the lord of the rākṣasas.
t.7.28.11: Then Jayanta, the son of Śacī, enraged, likewise struck back on the field of battle at his charioteer and at that son of Rāvaṇa himself.
t.7.28.12: Then the enraged Rāvaṇi, the mighty and splendid rākṣasa, his eyes wide open, covered that son of Śakra with showers of arrows.
t.7.28.13: Then, taking up weapons both mighty and huge, Rāvaṇi hurled down śataghnīs, lances, darts, maces, swords and battle-axes, and enormous mountain peaks.
t.7.28.14: Then, as that son of Rāvaṇa struck down his enemies, the worlds were thrown into deep distress, and a great darkness arose.
t.7.28.15: Then that army of the gods ran about here and there in many ways on every side around that son of Śacī, who was in distress.
t.7.28.16: Then they could not recognize one another, whether enemies or gods; here and there, in utter confusion, there was running about on every side.
t.7.28.17: Meanwhile, a heroic and mighty Daitya named Pulomā seized the son of Śacī and carried him away.
t.7.28.18: Taking that grandson with him, his maternal grandfather, the venerable one from whom Śacī has her name Paulomī, entered the great ocean.
t.7.28.19: But the gods, seeing the most dreadful disappearance of Jayanta, were distressed and dejected, and fled in all directions.
t.7.28.20: Then Rāvaṇi, thrilled with delight and surrounded by his own forces, rushed upon those gods and let out a mighty roar.
t.7.28.21: Seeing the disappearance of his son and also the valour of Rāvaṇi, the lord of the gods said to Mātali, "Let the chariot be brought."
t.7.28.22: That great chariot, divine and exceedingly terrifying, already fully equipped and swift as thought, arrived, driven by Mātali.
t.7.28.23: Then, as that chariot went on, clouds charged with lightning and loud-roaring, tossed swiftly by the wind, moving out in front, thundered aloud.
t.7.28.24: As Vāsava set out for battle, various musical instruments were played, well-composed hymns of praise were recited, and troupes of Apsarases danced.
t.7.28.25: Surrounded by the Rudras, the Vasus, the Ādityas, the Sādhyas and the hosts of Maruts, all bearing various weapons, the lord of the thirty gods went forth.
t.7.28.26: As Śakra was setting forth, the wind blew harshly, the sun became lustreless, and great meteors fell.
t.7.28.27: Meanwhile the heroic and mighty Daśagrīva mounted his divine chariot, fashioned by Viśvakarman.
t.7.28.28: It was encircled by hair-raising serpents of enormous size, by the wind of whose breath the battlefield seemed set ablaze.
t.7.28.29: Surrounded by valiant Daityas and night-roamers, the divine chariot, turned toward battle, advanced against the great Indra.
t.7.28.30: Having held back that son of his, he himself took his stand for battle; and Rāvaṇi too, withdrawing from the fight, sat down.
t.7.28.31: Then a battle broke out between the gods and the Rākṣasas, a terrible downpour of weapons in the fray, like that of clouds.
t.7.28.32: But the evil-minded Kumbhakarṇa, raising various weapons, could not be made out in the battle at that time; he was fighting with someone or other.
t.7.28.33: Enraged, he struck the gods with whatever came to hand: with his teeth, with his two arms and two feet, and with spears, lances and arrows.
t.7.28.34: Then the night-roamer, having joined battle with the illustrious Rudras together with the Ādityas, was cut by them in the fight with weapons without respite.
t.7.28.35: Then that entire Rākṣasa army was put to flight in battle by the thirty gods together with the hosts of Maruts, wielding sharp weapons of many kinds.
t.7.28.36: Some, struck down by weapons, writhed upon the surface of the earth, while others, clinging to their mounts, remained just as they were in the battle.
t.7.28.37: Chariots, elephants, donkeys, camels, serpents and horses, as well as dolphins, boars, and creatures with the faces of piśācas.
t.7.28.39: That tumult of battle, with the rākṣasas lying slain upon the surface of the earth, struck down while heedless, looked like a painted picture.
t.7.28.38: Some of the night-rangers, clasping them in their arms, stood rigid and upright; but, pierced through by the weapons of the gods, the night-rangers died.
t.7.28.40: At the forefront of the battle there began to flow a river whose streaming waters were blood, thronged with herons and vultures, and with weapons for its crocodiles.
t.7.28.41: Meanwhile, the mighty Daśagrīva, having seen that entire army of his struck down by the gods, became enraged.
t.7.28.42: Swiftly plunging into that swollen ocean of an army, he struck down the gods in battle and advanced straight against Śakra himself.
t.7.28.43: Then Śakra drew his great bow of tremendous sound, and at the twang of its drawing the ten directions resounded.
t.7.28.44: Drawing that mighty bow, Indra rained down upon Rāvaṇa's head arrows blazing with the splendour of fire and the sun.
t.7.28.45: And in the same way the mighty-armed Daśagrīva, standing firm, covered Śakra with showers of arrows loosed from his bow.
t.7.28.46: Then, as those two fought on with showers of arrows on every side, nothing at all could be discerned, for everything was shrouded in darkness.
